questions.question: Complete the Born-Haber cycle for CaCl2 by writing the formulae, with state symbols and relevant electrons, on the horizontal lines. The cycle diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Levels from the bottom up: Ca(s) + Cl2(g); Ca(g) + Cl2(g); Ca(g) + 2Cl(g); Ca+(g) + e- + 2Cl(g); Ca2+(g) + 2e- + 2Cl(g); then (right side) Ca2+(g) + 2Cl-(g)
steps: deltaH2 (atomisation of Ca): the line above Ca(s) + Cl2(g) is Ca(g) + Cl2(g).
deltaH3 (atomisation of chlorine, 2 x +121.7): the next line is Ca(g) + 2Cl(g).
deltaH4 (first ionisation energy of Ca): the next line is Ca+(g) + e- + 2Cl(g).
deltaH5 (second ionisation energy of Ca): the top line is Ca2+(g) + 2e- + 2Cl(g).
deltaH6 is 2 x the electron affinity of Cl (down to Ca2+(g) + 2Cl-(g)); deltaH7 is the lattice energy; deltaH1 is the enthalpy change of formation.

questions.question: Using the cycle and the table of values, calculate the second ionisation energy of calcium, including sign and units. The table values are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: second ionisation energy of calcium = +1148 kJ mol-1
steps: Hess's law: deltaH1 = deltaH2 + deltaH3 + deltaH4 + deltaH5 + deltaH6 + deltaH7.
The known terms add to 178.2 + 243.4 + 590.0 - 697.6 - 2258 = -1944.0, so IE2 = -795.8 + 1944.0 = +1148.2 kJ mol-1 (about +1148 kJ mol-1, positive because it is endothermic).

questions.question: The theoretical lattice energy of CaCl2 is -2223 kJ mol-1. Explain why the experimental (Born-Haber) lattice energy is more exothermic than this theoretical value.
questions.answer: The theoretical value assumes purely ionic bonding; the real compound has covalent character from polarisation of Cl- by Ca2+, giving a more exothermic experimental value
steps: The theoretical lattice energy is calculated from electrostatics, assuming perfectly spherical ions and purely ionic bonding.
Calcium ions have a high charge density (2+ and small), so they polarise the large chloride ions.
This polarisation gives the bonding some covalent character, which the ionic model does not include.
The extra covalent bonding makes the lattice more stable, so the experimental lattice energy is more exothermic than -2223 kJ mol-1.

questions.question: Explain the trend in theoretical lattice energies of the Group 2 chlorides on descending Group 2.
questions.answer: Lattice energy becomes less exothermic down the group because the cations get larger, so charge density falls and the electrostatic attraction weakens
steps: Going down Group 2, the metal ions get larger because they have more electron shells.
The 2+ charge stays the same, so the charge density (charge/radius) decreases.
Weaker attraction between the larger cation and the chloride ions means less energy is released when the lattice forms.
So the lattice energy becomes less exothermic on descending the group.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Change Of Solution Of CaCl2
questions.question: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of CaCl2 using the experimental lattice energy of -2258 kJ mol-1. The hydration enthalpies needed are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: enthalpy change of solution of CaCl2 = -120 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH(sol) = -(lattice energy) + deltaH(hyd, Ca2+) + 2 x deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.question: In a Born-Haber cycle for LiCl, what does the labelled energy change X represent? Options: A sum of hydration enthalpies of gaseous ions, B enthalpy change of formation of LiCl, C enthalpy change of solution of LiCl, D lattice energy of LiCl. The diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: A: the sum of the enthalpy changes of hydration of the gaseous ions
steps: X is the arrow from Li+(g) + Cl-(g) to Li+(aq) + Cl-(aq): the gaseous ions are dissolved in water.
This is deltaH(hyd, Li+) + deltaH(hyd, Cl-); the other arrows are the lattice energy (gaseous ions to LiCl(s)) and the enthalpy change of solution (LiCl(s) to aqueous ions).

questions.topic: Electron Affinity Of Chlorine From Cycle
questions.question: For the Born-Haber cycle for MgCl2 (energy changes labelled w, x, y, etc.), which expression gives the electron affinity of chlorine? Options: A y, B y/2, C (w + y), D (w + y)/2. The diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: y/2
steps: y is the step Mg2+(g) + 2e- + 2Cl(g) -> Mg2+(g) + 2Cl-(g), which adds one electron to each of two Cl atoms.
The electron affinity of chlorine is for one mole of atoms, so it equals y/2.

questions.question: Which expression gives the lattice energy of magnesium chloride from the labelled cycle? Options: A LE = u - (v + w + x + y), B LE = v + w + x + y - u, C LE = y - u - (v + w + x), D LE = v + w + x - y + u.
questions.answer: A: LE = u - (v + w + x + y)
steps: By Hess's law the route round the cycle gives u = v + w + x + y + LE (all signed values).
Rearranging: LE = u - (v + w + x + y).

questions.question: Which energy change in the MgCl2 cycle does x represent? Options: A first ionisation energy of Mg, B second ionisation energy of Mg, C sum of first and second ionisation energies of Mg, D sum of the enthalpy change of atomisation and the first and second ionisation energies of Mg. The diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: the sum of the first and second ionisation energies of magnesium
steps: x is the step Mg(g) -> Mg2+(g) + 2e-.
That removes two electrons from the gaseous atom: IE1 + IE2 of magnesium.

questions.question: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of bromine? The four options are shown in the figure below.
steps: Enthalpy change of atomisation is for the formation of one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state.
Bromine is a liquid under standard conditions, so the equation is 1/2 Br2(l) -> Br(g).
B makes two moles of atoms; C and D start from Br2(g), which is not the standard state.

questions.topic: Data Not Needed For Solution Enthalpy
questions.question: The enthalpy change of solution of Na2SO4 is calculated from three pieces of data. Which is NOT required? Options: A lattice energy of Na2SO4, B enthalpy change of hydration of Na+, C enthalpy change of formation of Na2SO4, D enthalpy change of hydration of SO4^2- (text partly missing).
questions.answer: C - enthalpy change of formation of Na2SO4
steps: The enthalpy change of solution cycle uses: lattice energy (breaking the lattice), and the hydration enthalpies of the ions formed.
Lattice energy (A) is needed to break the solid lattice.
Hydration enthalpies of Na+ (B) and SO4^2- (D) are needed for the ions in solution.
The enthalpy change of formation of Na2SO4 (C) is not part of the solution cycle, so it is not required.

questions.question: Which compound would be expected to have the least exothermic lattice energy? Options: A calcium chloride, B magnesium chloride, C potassium bromide, D sodium bromide.
questions.answer: C - potassium bromide
steps: Lattice energy depends on the charges of the ions (product of charges) and on the ionic radii.
CaCl2 and MgCl2 have 2+ cations, so their lattice energies are very exothermic.
KBr and NaBr have 1+ and 1- ions, so they are much less exothermic.
K+ is larger than Na+, so its charge density is lower and the lattice energy is less exothermic.
So potassium bromide has the least exothermic lattice energy, option C.

questions.question: Which compound would be expected to have the largest difference between experimental (Born-Haber) and theoretical lattice energies? Options: A calcium chloride, B magnesium chloride, C potassium bromide, D sodium bromide.
questions.answer: B - magnesium chloride
steps: The difference between experimental and theoretical values is largest when the bonding has the most covalent character.
Covalent character increases with the polarising power of the cation (high charge and small size).
Mg2+ is the smallest and most highly charged cation of the four, so it has the greatest polarising power.
So MgCl2 has the most covalent character and the largest difference, option B.

questions.question: The standard enthalpy change of solution of KCl is +17 kJ mol-1 and its solubility is 359 g dm-3 at 298 K. Which explains the solubility? Options: A hydration enthalpy of K+ and lattice energy of KCl are exothermic, B (garbled option about enthalpy values), C total entropy change on dissolving is positive, D total entropy change on dissolving is negative.
questions.answer: C - the total entropy change when KCl dissolves is positive
steps: The enthalpy change of solution is endothermic (+17 kJ mol-1), so enthalpy alone does not favour dissolving.
Dissolving disperses the ions into solution, which increases the entropy of the system.
The entropy of the surroundings also changes as the solution cools, so the total entropy change can be positive.
A positive total entropy change makes dissolving feasible, so option C is the explanation.

questions.question: Using the theoretical and experimental (Born-Haber) lattice energies of NaCl and MgI2 in the table, compare and contrast the type and strength of bonding in the two compounds, giving reasons. The table is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: NaCl is almost purely ionic (theoretical and experimental values agree); MgI2 has a lot of covalent character (experimental much more exothermic), although both are ionic lattices
steps: NaCl: theoretical -770 and experimental -780 kJ mol-1 differ by only about 1%, so the ionic model (point charges, perfect spheres) fits and the bonding is almost completely ionic.
MgI2: theoretical -1944 and experimental -2327 kJ mol-1 differ by about 20%, so it has significant covalent character.

Reason: Mg2+ is small and 2+ (high charge density), so it polarises the large, easily polarised I- ion, drawing some electron density between the nuclei; this extra covalent bonding makes the real lattice energy more exothermic than the theoretical value.
Na+ is larger with only 1+ charge and Cl- is smaller and less polarisable, so there is little polarisation.
Strength: MgI2 has the larger (more exothermic) lattice energy in both columns because of the 2+ ion charge, so its bonding is stronger overall, despite the larger anion.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Of Atomisation Of Iodine Equation
questions.question: The enthalpy change of atomisation of iodine (+107 kJ mol-1) is given by which equation? Options: A 1/2 I2(g) -> I(g), B 1/2 I2(s) -> I(g), C I2(g) -> 2I(g), D I2(s) -> 2I(g).
steps: Atomisation is the formation of 1 mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state.
Atomisation is written from the gaseous element, so the starting species is I2(g) for this cycle.
The equation is per mole of atoms, so 1/2 I2 gives 1 mole of I(g).
This matches option A.

questions.topic: Electron Affinity Of Iodine From Cycle
questions.question: Using the simplified Born-Haber cycle for LiI, calculate the electron affinity of iodine. Options: A -298, B -242, C +242, D +298 kJ mol-1. The cycle values are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: A: -298 kJ mol-1
steps: Enthalpy change of formation of LiI (the diagonal arrow) = -270 = sum of the steps round the cycle.
The known terms add to +28, so EA = -270 - 28 = -298 kJ mol-1 (exothermic).

questions.question: Using a table of energy changes, calculate the enthalpy change of hydration of Ca2+(g). Options: A -1410, B -1650, C -2014, D -3106 kJ mol-1. The table is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: -1650 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH(sol) = -(lattice energy) + deltaH(hyd, Ca2+) + 2 x deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.topic: True Statement About Hydration And Solution
questions.question: Which statement is true? A The enthalpy change of hydration of an ion is always negative; B the enthalpy change of solution of an ionic compound is always negative; C an endothermic enthalpy change of solution means the compound is insoluble; D the more exothermic the lattice energy, the more soluble the compound.
questions.answer: A - the enthalpy change of hydration of an ion is always negative
steps: Hydration is the process of an ion becoming surrounded by water molecules, which releases energy as ion-dipole bonds form.
So the enthalpy change of hydration is always exothermic, i.e. negative (option A is true).
The enthalpy change of solution can be positive (endothermic), as for KCl, so B is false.
An endothermic solution does not mean insoluble, so C is false; a more exothermic lattice energy makes solubility less likely, so D is false.

questions.question: Which compound would show the largest percentage difference between experimental and theoretical lattice energies? The ionic radii and charges are in a table shown in the figure below. Options: A PR, B PS, C QR, D QS.
questions.answer: B: PS
steps: The difference between experimental and theoretical lattice energies increases with the amount of covalent character, which depends on how strongly the anion is polarised.
Polarisation is greatest for a small cation (high charge density) with a large, easily polarised anion; P+ is the smallest cation (0.076 nm) and S- is the largest anion (0.220 nm).
So PS shows the largest percentage difference.

questions.question: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon, Fe2O3(s) + 3C(s) -> 2Fe(s) + 3CO(g), using the data given.
steps: deltaH(r) = sum of deltaH(f, products) - sum of deltaH(f, reactants).

questions.question: Calculate the entropy change of the system for the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon using the given data.
questions.answer: deltaS(system) = +542.9 J K-1 mol-1
steps: deltaS(system) = sum of S(products) - sum of S(reactants).

questions.question: Using your answers from (a)(i) and (a)(ii), calculate the temperature at which the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon becomes feasible.
questions.answer: T = about 908 K (about 635 C)
steps: The reaction becomes feasible when deltaS(total) = deltaS(system) - deltaH/T is no longer negative (limit: deltaS(total) = 0).
So T = deltaH / deltaS(system) = 492 700 J mol-1 / 542.9 J K-1 mol-1 (convert kJ to J).
T = 908 K (907.5 K, or about 635 C).

questions.question: The reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide has deltaH = -24.8 kJ mol-1 and deltaS = +15.2 J mol-1 K-1. Explain why the reaction should be feasible at any temperature.
questions.answer: deltaH is negative and deltaS is positive, so deltaG = deltaH - T deltaS is negative at all temperatures
steps: Feasibility requires deltaG = deltaH - T deltaS to be negative.
deltaH = -24.8 kJ mol-1 is negative, so the first term always makes deltaG negative.
deltaS = +15.2 J mol-1 K-1 is positive, so -T deltaS is also negative for any temperature above 0 K.
Both terms are negative, so deltaG is negative at all temperatures and the reaction is feasible at any temperature.

questions.topic: Effect Of Temperature On Total Entropy
questions.question: Explain how an increase in temperature would affect the total entropy change of the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide. No calculation is required.
questions.answer: The total entropy change decreases with rising temperature, because the surroundings term (-deltaH/T) gets smaller while the system term stays constant
steps: deltaStotal = deltaSsystem + deltaSsurroundings.
deltaSsystem = +15.2 J K-1 mol-1 is constant with temperature.
deltaSsurroundings = -deltaH / T = +24 800 / T, which is positive but gets smaller as T increases.
So deltaStotal falls as T increases, although it stays positive and the reaction remains feasible.

questions.question: Complete the Born-Haber cycle for iron(II) oxide by putting letters in the boxes to label the energy changes. The diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Bottom-left box: D; then going up the left side: A (atomisation of Fe), B (first IE of Fe), C (given), H (atomisation of oxygen); right side: E (first EA of O), F (second EA of O), G (lattice energy, long arrow down to FeO(s))
steps: D is the enthalpy change of formation: the arrow from Fe(s) + 1/2 O2(g) down to FeO(s).
Left-hand arrows going up: A (Fe(s) -> Fe(g)), B (Fe(g) -> Fe+(g)), C (given: Fe+ -> Fe2+), H (1/2 O2(g) -> O(g)).
Right side: E for Fe2+(g) + O(g) -> Fe2+(g) + O-(g) (first electron affinity), F for O-(g) -> O2-(g) (second electron affinity), and G for the long arrow Fe2+(g) + O2-(g) -> FeO(s) (lattice energy).

questions.question: Calculate the value for the second ionisation energy of iron, C, from the Born-Haber cycle for FeO. The data are in a table shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: second ionisation energy of iron, C = +1567 kJ mol-1
steps: Hess's law: D = A + B + C + H + E + F + G.
The known terms add to -1839, so C = -272 + 1839 = +1567 kJ mol-1.

questions.topic: Positive Second Electron Affinity Of Oxygen
questions.question: Suggest why the second electron affinity of oxygen is positive.
questions.answer: The added electron is repelled by the negative O- ion, so energy must be supplied to add it
steps: The first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic because O atoms attract an extra electron.
The second electron must be added to the negatively charged O- ion.
The O- ion repels the incoming electron electrostatically.
Energy must be supplied to overcome this repulsion, so the second electron affinity is positive (endothermic).

questions.question: For the Born-Haber cycle of SrI2 (values in kJ mol-1, not to scale), which statement is not true? Options: A lattice energy is exothermic, B first electron affinity of iodine is -295, C second ionisation energy of strontium is +1614, D standard enthalpy change of atomisation of strontium is +164. The cycle diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: the second ionisation energy of strontium is +1614 kJ mol-1 (this is not true)
steps: The +1614 kJ mol-1 arrow goes from Sr(g) + 2I(g) to Sr2+(g) + 2I(g) + 2e-: two electrons are removed, so +1614 is the sum of the first and second ionisation energies, not the second alone.
A is true (-1963 is exothermic); B is true (-590 / 2 = -295); D is true (+164 on the Sr(s) -> Sr(g) arrow).

questions.question: Using the Born-Haber cycle for SrI2, calculate the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of iodine. Options: A +542, B +271, C +214, D +107 kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: D: +107 kJ mol-1
steps: The known terms add to -775, so I2(s) -> 2I(g) = -561 + 775 = +214 kJ mol-1.
Atomisation of iodine is defined per mole of atoms, 1/2 I2(s) -> I(g), so it is 214 / 2 = +107 kJ mol-1.

questions.question: Which is most likely to be the theoretical lattice energy of strontium iodide, calculated assuming only ionic bonding? Options: A -561, B -1937, C -1963, D -1989 kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: B: -1937 kJ mol-1
steps: The Born-Haber (experimental) lattice energy is -1963 kJ mol-1, and SrI2 has some covalent character (large polarisable I-).
Covalent character makes the experimental value more exothermic than the purely ionic theoretical value, so the theoretical value must be less exothermic than -1963.
Only -1937 fits (-1989 is more exothermic and -561 is far too small).

questions.question: State the value of the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of calcium from the Born-Haber cycle for calcium chloride. The cycle is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: +178 kJ mol-1
steps: The arrow Ca(s) + Cl2(g) -> Ca(g) + Cl2(g) is the atomisation of calcium.
Its value on the cycle is +178 kJ mol-1.

questions.question: Calculate the enthalpy change of formation of calcium chloride from the Born-Haber cycle. The values are in the diagram, shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: deltaH(f, CaCl2) = -799 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH(f) = sum of all steps in the cycle: atomisation Ca + IE1 + IE2 + 2 x atomisation Cl + 2 x EA + lattice energy.

questions.question: Explain why the difference between theoretical and experimental lattice energy is much greater for calcium iodide than for calcium chloride.
questions.answer: The large iodide ion is easily polarised by Ca2+, so CaI2 has much more covalent character than CaCl2, which the ionic model does not include
steps: Theoretical lattice energy assumes purely ionic bonding with spherical ions.
The difference between theoretical and experimental values is caused by covalent character from polarisation of the anion.
Iodide is a very large anion with a diffuse electron cloud, so it is highly polarisable.
Chloride is smaller and less polarisable, so CaCl2 is much closer to ionic.
CaI2 therefore has far more covalent character, giving a much larger difference between the theoretical and experimental values.

questions.question: Complete the energy cycle for dissolving calcium chloride in water, including the labelled arrows. The cycle diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Empty box: Ca2+(g) + 2Cl-(g), joined by an arrow labelled lattice energy to CaCl2(s) and an arrow labelled sum of hydration enthalpies to Ca2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq)
steps: Write Ca2+(g) + 2Cl-(g) in the empty box under the cycle.
Draw the arrow from this box to CaCl2(s), labelled lattice energy (LE = -2258 kJ mol-1).
Draw the arrow from the box to Ca2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq), labelled deltaH(hyd, Ca2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-) (sum of the hydration enthalpies).
The existing arrow CaCl2(s) -> Ca2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) is deltaH(sol).

questions.topic: Enthalpy Change Of Solution Of CaCl2
questions.question: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of calcium chloride using the completed energy cycle in (d)(i).
questions.answer: deltaH(sol, CaCl2) = -77 kJ mol-1
steps: From the cycle: deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Ca2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.question: An ionic compound has some covalent bonding. What causes the covalency, and how does the lattice energy from a Born-Haber cycle differ from the theoretical electrostatic value? The option list is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: anion polarised by cation; Born-Haber lattice energy more exothermic than the theoretical value
steps: Covalent character arises when the cation (small, highly charged) distorts, i.e. polarises, the electron cloud of the large anion.
This sharing of electron density adds extra bonding that the purely ionic model leaves out, so the experimental (Born-Haber) lattice energy is more exothermic than the theoretical value.

questions.topic: Energy Change Y In Sodium Oxide Cycle
questions.question: Which energy change in the Born-Haber cycle for sodium oxide does y represent? Options: A first electron affinity of oxygen, B second electron affinity of oxygen, C sum of the first and second electron affinities of oxygen, D sum of the enthalpy change of atomisation of oxygen and the first and second electron affinities of oxygen. The diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: the sum of the first and second electron affinities of oxygen
steps: y goes from 2Na+(g) + 2e- + O(g) to 2Na+(g) + O2-(g): the oxygen atom gains two electrons.
That is EA1 (O -> O-) plus EA2 (O- -> O2-).

questions.topic: Enthalpy Of Formation Expression For Sodium Oxide
questions.question: Which expression gives the enthalpy change of formation of sodium oxide? Options: A v + w + x - y - z, B v + w + x + y - z, C v + w + x - y + z, D v + w + x + y + z.
questions.answer: D: deltaH(f) = v + w + x + y + z
steps: u is the enthalpy change of formation of Na2O, and the longer route round the cycle is v + w + x + y + z.
By Hess's law, u = v + w + x + y + z, with each value used with its own sign.

questions.question: Identify the missing details represented by the letters R and W in the Born-Haber cycle for barium oxide. The cycle diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: R = O2-(g); W = first electron affinity of oxygen (O(g) + e- -> O-(g))
steps: R: the top level is reached from Ba2+(g) + O-(g) by the second electron affinity of O-, so R is O2-(g).
W: the arrow from Ba2+(g) + O(g) down to Ba2+(g) + O-(g) is the gain of one electron by an oxygen atom, i.e. the first electron affinity of oxygen.

questions.topic: Calculating Value Z In BaO Cycle
questions.question: Use the data given to calculate a value for quantity Z in the Born-Haber cycle for barium oxide, including sign and units. The data are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: deltaZ = deltaH(f, BaO) = -499.9 kJ mol-1
steps: Z is the enthalpy change of formation: deltaZ = atomisation Ba + atomisation O + IE1 + IE2 + deltaW + EA2 + LE.
= -499.9 kJ mol-1 (about -500 kJ mol-1, exothermic).

questions.topic: Agreement Of Theoretical And Experimental Values
questions.question: The table gives lattice energies of barium oxide and magnesium iodide and the percentage difference between theoretical and experimental values. Explain why there is closer agreement for barium oxide than for magnesium iodide.
questions.answer: BaO is more ionic: the oxide ion is small and highly charged but not very polarisable, while MgI2 has a small cation and a large polarisable iodide ion, giving more covalent character
steps: Theoretical lattice energies assume purely ionic bonding with spherical ions.
Barium oxide is made of a large, low-charge-density Ba2+ ion and the small O2- ion, so the bonding is close to purely ionic.
Magnesium iodide has a small, highly polarising Mg2+ ion and a large, easily polarised I- ion.
Polarisation adds covalent character to MgI2, so the real lattice energy differs much more from the ionic theoretical value.
Hence agreement is closer for barium oxide than for magnesium iodide.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Of Solution Of Ba(OH)2 By Hess Cycle
questions.question: Using a fully labelled Hess cycle and the hydration enthalpy of OH- (-460 kJ mol-1), calculate the enthalpy change of solution of Ba(OH)2. The table data are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: deltaH(sol, Ba(OH)2) = -50 kJ mol-1
steps: Hess cycle: Ba(OH)2(s) -> Ba2+(g) + 2OH-(g) (-LE, +2230 kJ mol-1), then Ba2+(g) + 2OH-(g) -> Ba2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) (sum of the hydration enthalpies); the direct route is deltaH(sol).
deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Ba2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, OH-).

questions.question: Explain why strontium hydroxide is slightly soluble in water even though its enthalpy change of solution is endothermic.
questions.answer: Dissolving increases the entropy of the system as ions disperse, so the total entropy change can be positive and dissolving is feasible despite the endothermic enthalpy change
steps: An endothermic enthalpy change of solution (deltaH positive) alone would not favour dissolving.
Dissolving disperses the ions through the solution, so the entropy of the system increases.
The total entropy change (system plus surroundings) can therefore be positive, so the process is feasible to a small extent.
Because the solubility is only slight, the favourable entropy term is limited by the endothermic enthalpy term.

questions.topic: True Statement About Lead Nitrate Cycle
questions.question: For the enthalpy cycle of lead(II) nitrate, which statement is true? Options: A enthalpy change of formation is -2151 kJ mol-1, B enthalpy change of solution is exothermic, C hydration of Pb2+ is more exothermic than that of NO3-, D entropy change of surroundings for dissolving is positive. The cycle values are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: the enthalpy change of hydration of a lead(II) ion is more exothermic than that of a nitrate ion
steps: Pb2+ hydration is -1485 kJ mol-1, whereas each nitrate ion has only about -314 kJ mol-1 (see part (b)), so C is true.

A is false: -2151 kJ mol-1 is the lattice energy, not the enthalpy change of formation; B is false: deltaH(sol) = +38 is endothermic; D is false: an endothermic dissolving process gives a negative entropy change of the surroundings (deltaS = -deltaH/T).

questions.question: Using the enthalpy cycle for lead(II) nitrate, calculate the enthalpy change of hydration of a nitrate ion. Options: A -3598, B -1799, C -628, D -314 kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: D: -314 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Pb2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, NO3-).
deltaH(hyd, NO3-) = -628 / 2 = -314 kJ mol-1.

questions.topic: Entropy Change For Barium Carbonate Decomposition
questions.question: Calculate the standard entropy change of the system for BaCO3(s) -> BaO(s) + CO2(g). The standard entropy data are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: deltaS(system) = +171.9 J K-1 mol-1
steps: deltaS(system) = S(BaO) + S(CO2) - S(BaCO3).

questions.question: The lowest temperature at which barium carbonate decomposes is 712 C. Using this and your answer to (a)(i), calculate the standard enthalpy change of the reaction, with an appropriate number of significant figures.
questions.answer: deltaH = +169 kJ mol-1
steps: At the lowest temperature of decomposition deltaS(total) = 0, so deltaS(system) = deltaH/T and deltaH = T x deltaS(system).
Convert and round to 3 s.f. (the temperature is given to 3 s.f.): deltaH = +169 kJ mol-1.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Of Solution Of MgCl2 From Calorimetry
questions.question: 4.26 g of anhydrous MgCl2 is dissolved in 200 cm3 of deionised water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 6.8 C. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of MgCl2, with sign and units. Specific heat capacity of the solution = 4.18 J g-1 C-1.
questions.answer: deltaH(sol) = about -130 kJ mol-1 (taking the solution mass as 204.26 g; about -127 kJ mol-1 if only 200 g is used)
steps: Mass of solution = 200 g water + 4.26 g MgCl2 = 204.26 g (taking 200 cm3 water as 200 g).
Heat absorbed by solution: q = m c deltaT = 204.26 x 4.18 x 6.8 = 5806 J.
Heat released by dissolving = 5806 J (the solution warmed, so the process is exothermic).
Molar mass of MgCl2 = 95.3 g mol-1, so moles = 4.26 / 95.3 = 0.0447 mol.

questions.question: Complete the Hess cycle for the enthalpy change of solution of anhydrous MgCl2 by adding formulae with state symbols to the empty boxes. The cycle diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Left box: Mg2+(g) + 2Cl-(g); right box: MgCl2(s)
steps: The arrow labelled lattice energy points from the left box to the right box, and lattice energy is the formation of the solid from gaseous ions: Mg2+(g) + 2Cl-(g) -> MgCl2(s).
The left box is also the start of the hydration arrow (gaseous ions to aqueous ions); the right box MgCl2(s) is the start of the solution arrow.

questions.question: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of hydration of chloride ions, using the Hess cycle in (c)(i) and your answer to (b). If (b) was not obtained, use -155 kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: deltaH(hyd, Cl-) = about -367 kJ mol-1 (using deltaH(sol) = -127 kJ mol-1 from part (b))
steps: Hess's law: deltaH(hyd, Mg2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-) = lattice energy + deltaH(sol).
deltaH(hyd, Cl-) = -733 / 2 = -367 kJ mol-1 (-368 if -130 kJ mol-1 is used for deltaH(sol); with the substitute value -155 it would be -381).

questions.question: Give two assumptions used in theoretical calculations of lattice energy.
questions.answer: Ions are perfect spheres (point charges) and the bonding is purely ionic with no covalent character
steps: Theoretical lattice energy is calculated electrostatically.
Assumption 1: the ions are perfect spheres with charge concentrated at the centre (point charges).
Assumption 2: the bonding is purely ionic, so there is no covalent character from polarisation.

questions.topic: Theoretical Versus Experimental Lattice Energy For MgCl2
questions.question: Explain the difference between the theoretical lattice energy of MgCl2 (-2326 kJ mol-1) and the experimental (Born-Haber) value.
questions.answer: The real MgCl2 has covalent character from polarisation of Cl- by the small, highly charged Mg2+, which the ionic theoretical value ignores
steps: The theoretical value assumes perfect ionic bonding with point charges.
Mg2+ is small and highly charged, so it has a high polarising power.
It distorts the electron cloud of the large Cl- ions, giving the bonds covalent character.
The covalent character adds extra stability, so the experimental lattice energy is more exothermic than the theoretical value.

questions.question: A 5.00 g sample of barium carbonate reacts with 120 cm3 of 0.500 mol dm-3 HCl. Show that the hydrochloric acid is in excess. BaCO3 + 2HCl + nH2O -> BaCl2.nH2O + CO2 + H2O.
questions.answer: 0.0253 mol BaCO3 needs 0.0507 mol HCl; 0.0600 mol HCl is available, so HCl is in excess
steps: Moles HCl needed = 2 x 0.0253 = 0.0507 mol.
Moles HCl supplied = 0.120 dm3 x 0.500 mol dm-3 = 0.0600 mol.
0.0600 mol is more than 0.0507 mol, so HCl is in excess.

questions.topic: Relative Formula Mass And Water Of Crystallisation
questions.question: All the barium carbonate reacted to give 6.19 g of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl2.nH2O. Calculate the relative formula mass of BaCl2.nH2O and hence deduce n.
steps: Moles of BaCl2.nH2O = moles of BaCO3 = 5.00 / 197.3 = 0.02534 mol (1:1 mole ratio).
Mass of water = 244.3 - 208.3 = 36.0 g mol-1, which is 2 x 18.0.
So n = 2.

questions.question: Complete the Born-Haber cycle for MgCl2 by adding labels for the four energy changes and writing formulae in the two empty boxes. The table and cycle are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Labels: B (first IE of Mg), C (second IE of Mg), D (atomisation of chlorine), E (lattice energy); empty boxes: Mg(g) + Cl2(g) (lower) and Mg+(g) + Cl2(g) + e- (upper)
steps: Box above Mg(s) + Cl2(g) (after the arrow A): Mg(g) + Cl2(g).
The arrow from Mg(g) + Cl2(g) to the next box is the first ionisation energy: label B; the next box is Mg+(g) + Cl2(g) + e-.
The arrow to Mg2+(g) + Cl2(g) + 2e- is the second ionisation energy: label C.
The top-left arrow Cl2(g) -> 2Cl(g) is the atomisation of chlorine: label D (a value of 2 x 122 is used for two Cl atoms).
The long right-hand arrow Mg2+(g) + 2Cl-(g) -> MgCl2(s) is the lattice energy: label E.

questions.topic: Electron Affinity Of Chlorine From Cycle
questions.question: Calculate the electron affinity of chlorine, in kJ mol-1, using the data in the table and the completed Born-Haber cycle for MgCl2.
questions.answer: electron affinity of chlorine = -348 kJ mol-1
steps: F = A + B + C + 2D + 2 x EA(Cl) + E (two Cl atoms are atomised and two are ionised).

questions.question: Explain why, when magnesium reacts with chlorine, MgCl2 is formed rather than MgCl3.
questions.answer: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+ with a noble gas configuration; removing a third electron needs a very large amount of energy that is not recovered in lattice formation
steps: Magnesium has two outer electrons; removing these gives Mg2+ with a stable noble gas (neon) arrangement.
Removing a third electron would require a very large third ionisation energy, from a stable inner shell.
The energy released by forming the extra lattice bonds is not large enough to pay for this third ionisation.
So the most stable product is MgCl2, not MgCl3.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Of Solution Of MgCl2 From Cycle
questions.question: Calculate the standard molar enthalpy change of solution of MgCl2 using the data shown and the lattice energy LE[MgCl2] from the table.
questions.answer: deltaH(sol, MgCl2) = -122 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Mg2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.topic: Structure And Bonding Versus Lattice Energy
questions.question: Discuss the reasons for the differences between the experimental and theoretical lattice energies of three crystal lattices, in terms of their structure and bonding. The six values are in a table shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: The theoretical value assumes 100% ionic bonding (perfect spherical ions); the experimental value includes real covalent character, which increases as the cation polarises the anion more. NaF is nearly ideal, MgF2 slightly less so, and MgCl2 differs most
steps: Theoretical values assume a purely ionic lattice of perfectly spherical ions held by electrostatic attraction; Born-Haber (experimental) values reflect the real bonding, including any covalent character.
NaF: -918 against -912 kJ mol-1. Na+ is large for a 1+ ion (low charge density) and F- is small and hard to polarise, so the bonding is almost completely ionic and the two values nearly agree.

MgF2: -2957 against -2913 kJ mol-1. Mg2+ is small and 2+, so it has high charge density and polarises F- slightly; a small amount of covalent character makes the experimental value a little more exothermic. Lattice energies are much larger than for NaF because of the 2+ charge.

MgCl2: -2526 against -2326 kJ mol-1. Cl- is bigger and more polarisable than F-, so Mg2+ distorts it considerably; the larger covalent contribution gives the biggest difference (experimental more exothermic).
Overall: the more the cation polarises the anion (high charge density cation, large anion), the more the experimental value exceeds the theoretical one.

questions.question: Which compound has the greatest degree of covalency within its ionic bonds? Options: A NaI, B AgBr, C Rb2S, D Li2O. The lattice energy data table is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: AgBr
steps: The greater the difference between the experimental and theoretical lattice energies, the greater the covalent character.
AgBr has by far the largest difference, so it has the most covalency.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Of Atomisation Of Iodine Equation
questions.question: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of iodine? The options are shown in the figure below.
steps: Atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state.
Iodine is a solid at standard conditions, so the equation is 1/2 I2(s) -> I(g); B and D are wrong state, C makes two moles of atoms.

questions.topic: Second Electron Affinity Of Oxygen Equation
questions.question: Which equation represents the second electron affinity of oxygen? The options are shown in the figure below.
steps: The second electron affinity is the gain of a second electron by a gaseous O- ion, forming O2-.
B adds two electrons to O (that is the sum of both electron affinities); C and D are ionisation energies.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate is thermodynamically feasible when considering the entropy of the system.
questions.answer: CO2 gas is formed (gas has high entropy), and the number of moles of gas/particles increases from 4 to 7
steps: Three moles of CO2 gas are formed, and gases have much higher entropy than solids or liquids.
The number of product particles (3 H2O + 3 CO2 + 1 Na3C6H5O7 = 7 mol) is greater than reactant particles (1 + 3 = 4 mol).
More particles give more ways of arranging energy and matter, so the entropy of the system increases.

questions.question: Describe, in terms of the particles involved, why the reaction does not occur until the tablets are dissolved in water.
questions.answer: In the solid the particles are fixed in position and cannot move to collide; dissolving frees the ions and molecules so they can move and collide
steps: In the solid tablet the citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate particles are held in fixed positions in a lattice.
They cannot move freely, so reactant particles rarely come into contact and collide.
When the tablet dissolves, the ions and molecules become mobile and disperse through the water.
Mobile particles collide frequently and with enough energy, so the reaction can then take place.

questions.question: For the reaction at 25 C, the standard entropy change of the surroundings is given in a value shown in the figure below. Calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction, including sign and units.
questions.answer: deltaH = +70.0 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaS(surroundings) = -deltaH / T, so deltaH = -T x deltaS(surroundings).
T = 25 + 273 = 298 K, deltaS(surroundings) = -234.9 J K-1 mol-1, so deltaH = -298 x (-234.9) = +70 000 J mol-1.
deltaH = +70.0 kJ mol-1 (endothermic, which is why the surroundings' entropy falls).

questions.question: Sketch an enthalpy level diagram showing the relationship between the enthalpy change of solution (+18.6 kJ mol-1 for NaHCO3), lattice energy and enthalpies of hydration, fully labelled.
questions.answer: Three levels: Na+(g) + HCO3-(g) at the top, Na+(aq) + HCO3-(aq) in the middle and NaHCO3(s) at the bottom; the aqueous ions are +18.6 kJ mol-1 above NaHCO3(s)
steps: Top level: Na+(g) + HCO3-(g). Bottom level: NaHCO3(s). Middle level: Na+(aq) + HCO3-(aq), 18.6 kJ above the solid.
Draw an arrow down from the top level to the bottom level, labelled lattice energy (exothermic, the longest arrow).
Draw an arrow down from the top level to the middle level, labelled sum of enthalpy changes of hydration (exothermic, a bit shorter than the lattice energy arrow).
Draw an arrow up from NaHCO3(s) to the middle level, labelled deltaH(sol) = +18.6 kJ mol-1 (endothermic, because |lattice energy| is larger than |sum of hydration enthalpies| by 18.6 kJ mol-1).

questions.question: Which compound has the greatest covalent character? Options: A CaBr2, B CaI2, C MgBr2, D MgI2.
questions.answer: D - MgI2
steps: Covalent character is greatest when the cation has high polarising power (small and highly charged) and the anion is large and easily polarised.
Mg2+ is smaller and more polarising than Ca2+.
I- is the largest and most polarisable halide of the options.
So MgI2 has the greatest covalent character, option D.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Change Of Dehydration Of CuSO4.5H2O
questions.question: Using the data in the table, calculate the standard enthalpy change for CuSO4.5H2O(s) -> CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l).
questions.answer: deltaH = +79.2 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH = sum of deltaH(f, products) - sum of deltaH(f, reactants).

questions.topic: Entropy Change Of Dehydration Of CuSO4.5H2O
questions.question: Using the data in the table, calculate the standard molar entropy change for CuSO4.5H2O(s) -> CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l).
questions.answer: deltaS(system) = +158.1 J K-1 mol-1
steps: deltaS = sum of S(products) - sum of S(reactants).

questions.question: Using your answers to (a)(i) and (a)(ii), calculate the lowest temperature at which hydrated copper(II) sulfate will decompose.
questions.answer: T = 501 K (about 228 C)
steps: The reaction starts to be feasible when deltaS(total) = deltaS(system) - deltaH/T = 0, so T = deltaH / deltaS(system).
T = 79 200 J mol-1 / 158.1 J K-1 mol-1 (convert kJ to J).

questions.question: A student dissolves 21.36 g of CuSO4.5H2O in 100 g of water and measures an enthalpy change of solution of +12.3 kJ mol-1. Using specific heat capacity 3.7 J g-1 C-1, total mass 121.36 g and molar mass 249.6 g mol-1, calculate the temperature change.
questions.answer: The temperature falls by 2.3 C (deltaT = -2.3 C) because the process is endothermic
steps: Moles of CuSO4.5H2O = 21.36 / 249.6 = 0.0856 mol.
Heat taken in = 12.3 kJ mol-1 x 0.0856 mol = 1.05 kJ = 1053 J (endothermic).
deltaT = 2.3 C, and because the solution absorbs heat, the temperature falls by 2.3 C.

questions.topic: Definition Of Enthalpy Change Of Hydration
questions.question: Explain what is meant by the term enthalpy change of hydration.
questions.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution (hydrated ions)
steps: It is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions is hydrated (surrounded by water molecules).
The process is done under standard conditions and forms an infinitely dilute solution.
It is always exothermic because bonds form between the ions and water molecules.

questions.question: Complete the Hess cycle for the enthalpy change of solution of CuCl2 by filling in the empty boxes. The cycle diagram is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Top box: Cu2+(g) + 2Cl-(g); left box: CuCl2(s)
steps: The lattice energy arrow goes from the gaseous ions to the solid, so the top box is Cu2+(g) + 2Cl-(g) and the left box is CuCl2(s).
The right-hand arrow from the top box to Cu2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) is the sum of the hydration enthalpies; the bottom arrow CuCl2(s) -> aqueous ions is deltaH(sol).

questions.topic: Expression For Enthalpy Change Of Solution
questions.question: Complete the expression for the enthalpy change of solution of CuCl2 using the enthalpy changes of hydration and the lattice energy: deltaH(sol) = ?
questions.answer: deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Cu2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-)
steps: Dissolving breaks the lattice: this takes in energy equal to -LE, since LE is negative.
Hydrating the ions releases energy: deltaH(hyd) for Cu2+ and for each Cl- (two Cl- ions).
So deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Cu2+) + 2 x deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.topic: Enthalpy Change Of Solution Of CuCl2
questions.question: The lattice energy of CuCl2 is -2811 kJ mol-1. Using this value, the data in the table and your expression in (c)(iii), calculate the enthalpy change of solution.
questions.answer: deltaH(sol, CuCl2) = -45 kJ mol-1
steps: deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Cu2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.question: The enthalpy change of hydration of Cu+ is -593 kJ mol-1. Explain why the hydration enthalpy of Cu+ is much less exothermic than that of Cu2+.
questions.answer: Cu+ has a lower charge (1+) than Cu2+ (2+), so it has a lower charge density and attracts water molecules less strongly
steps: Hydration enthalpy depends on the charge density of the ion (charge divided by radius).
Cu2+ has twice the charge of Cu+ for a similar size, so it has a much higher charge density.
Cu2+ therefore attracts water molecules more strongly and releases more energy on hydration.
Cu+ has a lower charge density, so its hydration enthalpy is much less exothermic.
